drink:The three Garnatxas.name: The three Garnatxas
drink:The three Garnatxas.teaser: Black, white and a dusky pink-grey: one grape family in three skins, and the Empordà bottles all of them
drink:The three Garnatxas.story: On the Empordà plain the old farmers called Garnatxa lledoner, and they grew it in every colour. Garnatxa negra makes most of the reds. Garnatxa blanca gives soft, floral whites. Between them sits lledoner roig, a berry that ripens to a dusty pink-grey and is pressed like a white; the DO Empordà lists it among its white grapes. Of roughly 61 hectares of it in Catalonia, about 60 grow here, so a bottle of it is close to a local exclusive. The vines are low bushes, many of them 50 to 120 years old, which give small crops of concentrated fruit.
drink:The three Garnatxas.why: Order a lledoner roig white once this week: you will rarely meet it bottled on its own anywhere else.
facts: Negra: ripe red fruit, warmth, a little spice. Blanca: white flowers and fennel. Roig: weight, texture and a salty edge, sometimes faintly oxidative
DO Empordà; Garnatxa negra, blanca, roja or gris, or the Catalan lledoner negre, blanc, roig; 'vinyes velles' for old vines

Un blanc de lledoner roig, or a negre of old-vine Garnatxa. Growers: Espelt at Vilajuïga and Mas Estela (both with their own cards in the larder), Vinyes dels Aspres at Cantallops; around €€ a bottle (seen Jun 2026)

drink:Carinyena.name: Carinyena
drink:Carinyena.teaser: Samsó to the old growers: the black grape that gives an Empordà red its grip and its acidity
drink:Carinyena.story: Carinyena is the second black grape of the Empordà, and on old farms it is still called Samsó. Its vines are tough, drought-proof bushes that crop little and hold their acidity through a hot August, which is exactly what Garnatxa lacks. In the old vineyards the two were planted side by side and picked together, and many Empordà reds are still a blend of both. Phylloxera wiped out the region's vines from 1879; the replanting that followed kept Carinyena in the mix. On its own it tastes of black cherry and bramble, with firm tannin and a sharp, food-friendly edge.
drink:Carinyena.why: Pick a Carinyena-led red when the table orders grilled meat or a black rice; its acidity cuts the fat.
facts: Dark fruit, black cherry and bramble; firm tannin and bright acidity; old vines add depth
DO Empordà; Carinyena or Samsó, often blended with Garnatxa negra; 'vinyes velles' for old vines
Un negre amb Carinyena, or a Samsó on its own. Mas Estela grows it on Cap de Creus (its own card in the larder); around €€ a bottle (seen Jun 2026)

drink:Garnatxa de l'Empordà.name: Garnatxa de l'Empordà
drink:Garnatxa de l'Empordà.teaser: Grapes shrivelled by sun and north wind, stopped with spirit, then left in old casks for years
drink:Garnatxa de l'Empordà.story: This is the glass an Empordà farmhouse poured at the end of Sunday lunch. Pale Garnatxa, mostly the red-skinned roja with some blanca, is left on the vine or in the sun until the tramuntana has dried the berries to near-raisins. The must is so sweet that the makers halt fermentation with wine spirit, keeping the sugar in; strengths run from about 14 to 20 per cent, and one Perelada bottling sits at 15. The long-aged ones spend years in old barrels, slowly oxidising until they go amber and taste of dried fig, walnut and toffee. It has nothing in common with the dry reds of the same grape.
drink:Garnatxa de l'Empordà.why: Drink it with a hard sheep's cheese or carquinyolis biscuits, not with a fruit dessert.
facts: Amber to mahogany; dried fig, raisin, walnut, toffee; the older, the more oxidative
DO Empordà, Garnatxa de l'Empordà, vi dolç natural; often 500 ml; an age statement on the old soleras

drink:Cremat.name: Cremat
drink:Cremat.teaser: A clay bowl of rum on fire at the table, put out with coffee and ladled hot into small cups
drink:Cremat.story: The name just means burnt. Into a wide earthenware cassola go dark rum, sugar, a cinnamon stick, a curl of lemon peel and a few roasted coffee beans. Someone puts a match to it, and for several minutes the blue flame is stirred, lifted on the ladle and poured back, caramelising the sugar while part of the alcohol burns away. A jug of hot coffee goes in to kill the fire. What is left is served scalding in little cups: sweet, smoky, bitter at the edges. The rum is the trace of the nineteenth-century trade between this coast's ships and Cuba.
drink:Cremat.why: Have it lit at your own table on a cool night; the flame is half the drink.
facts: Hot and sweet: burnt sugar, coffee, cinnamon and lemon, the rum softened by the burning
Not a bottled drink: made in the bowl to order, mostly in summer at Calella de Palafrugell and along the coast
Un cremat per a la taula. Calella's Port Bo is its home ground; the songs sung over it have their own card under Listening

drink:Ratafia.name: Ratafia
drink:Ratafia.teaser: Unripe walnuts and garden herbs steeped in spirit: the dark, bittersweet glass after a long lunch
drink:Ratafia.story: Ratafia begins in early summer, when the walnuts are still green and soft enough to cut through, shell and all. They go into spirit with herbs and spices, and every family keeps its own list; at home the jars traditionally sit out in sun and dew for about forty days. The protected version, IGP Ratafia Catalana, is stricter: at least three months of maceration, then at least three more in wood, and a botanical mix that must include lemon verbena, cinnamon, clove and nutmeg. It comes out dark brown, sweet and slightly tannic from the walnut skins, at 24 to 30 per cent.
drink:Ratafia.why: Ask whether the house pours its own: a village ratafia from a plain bottle is often the best one on offer.
facts: Dark brown; green walnut, clove, cinnamon, herbs; sweet, with a bitter, drying finish
Ratafia Catalana IGP for the protected version; 24–30% vol.
Una ratafia, cool, with carquinyolis if there are any. Around €€ for 700 ml from small makers (seen Jun 2026)

listening:No hi-fi bar on this coast.name: No hi-fi bar on this coast
listening:No hi-fi bar on this coast.teaser: We looked for a vinyl or listening bar from Girona to Palafrugell and found none to send you to
listening:No hi-fi bar on this coast.story: Listening bars, the rooms built around a serious sound system and a wall of records, have spread from Tokyo to most big cities. This coast has not caught up. In October 2026 we searched Girona, Figueres and Palafrugell, in English and Catalan, through press, Time Out Girona and local listings, and turned up wine bars, cocktail bars, clubs and a jazz bar, but no room where the point is to sit and hear a record played well. The music here is live and mostly outdoors, and mostly in summer: opera in a castle garden, arena acts above the sea, sailors' songs on a beach.
listening:No hi-fi bar on this coast.why: Plan the music around the summer festivals instead; they are the real listening rooms of this coast.
facts: Nothing to visit: no hi-fi or vinyl listening bar found in Girona, Figueres or Palafrugell (searched Oct 2026)
The Peralada and Cap Roig festivals and the Calella havaneres, each with its own card here, all in July and August

listening:Festival Castell de Peralada.name: Festival Castell de Peralada
listening:Festival Castell de Peralada.teaser: Opera singers and ballet companies on an open-air stage in the gardens of the Peralada castle
listening:Festival Castell de Peralada.story: Every summer since 1987 the Peralada castle has turned its gardens into a theatre. The 40th edition opened on 17 July 2026 with tenor Benjamin Bernheim and soprano Ermonela Jaho in recital, and ran into August with opera, chamber music, baroque sacred music and dance; the festival's own young-dancer campus marked its tenth year with a new piece, Niu, danced with Hamburg Ballet artists at 22:00 on 28 July. Smaller concerts move indoors, to the Carme church and the winery. Arriving at dusk, you walk through the castle grounds with the heat going out of the day before the lights go down.
listening:Festival Castell de Peralada.why: Choose a garden-stage night rather than an indoor recital: the open-air auditorium is what you came for.
facts: Castell de Peralada, Peralada (Alt Empordà): gardens, Carme church, Mirador and the Perelada winery

listening:Cap Roig Festival.name: Cap Roig Festival
listening:Cap Roig Festival.teaser: International headliners on a stage in the clifftop gardens above Calella, the sea behind the band
listening:Cap Roig Festival.story: Cap Roig is where the coast books its arena names. The 26th edition ran from 3 July to 18 August 2026, 23 concerts in all: Bryan Adams opened, and Diana Krall, Mika, Anastacia and Rick Astley played alongside Spanish and Catalan acts such as Amaia and Luz Casal, before Miguel Ríos closed it with El último vals. The open-air auditorium sits inside the Cap Roig gardens between Calella de Palafrugell and Palamós, so the walk to your seat goes through pines and terraces. The 2026 line-up was presented on 27 February, with tickets on sale from 2 March.
listening:Cap Roig Festival.why: Book early in spring for a seat, and go for the setting as much as for the act.
facts: Jardins de Cap Roig, Calella de Palafrugell; the gardens have their own card under Linger

listening:The Cantada d'Havaneres.name: The Cantada d'Havaneres
listening:The Cantada d'Havaneres.teaser: Thousands on the sand at Port Bo singing Cuban-rhythm songs with the groups: in 2026, called off by a fire
listening:The Cantada d'Havaneres.story: Havaneres are slow, swaying songs in the habanera rhythm that Catalan sailors brought back from Cuba in the nineteenth century, and at Calella de Palafrugell they get one night a year on the beach. Since 1966 groups have sung from a stage at Port Bo while the crowd, more than 33,000 people at a recent edition, packs the sand and the rocks and joins the choruses. The 59th Cantada was set for Saturday 4 July 2026, with Cremats, Ultramar, Port-Bo and Arjau on the bill. That afternoon the organisers cancelled it on emergency-service advice because of a wildfire nearby; the only earlier cancellation was in 2020.
listening:The Cantada d'Havaneres.why: Come for the communal choruses near the end, when the whole beach sings with the groups.
facts: Platja del Port Bo, Calella de Palafrugell
Traditionally the first Saturday of July; the 2026 night (4 July) was cancelled for a wildfire. The 2027 date is not announced yet (Oct 2026)
Watching from the beach and rocks is open to all; seating arrangements change, check the Ajuntament's notice

around:Besalú.name: Besalú
around:Besalú.teaser: A fortified bridge over the Fluvià and, under the old Jewish quarter, a ritual bath found only in 1964
around:Besalú.story: Besalú announces itself from the road: a long Romanesque bridge kinked in the middle, with a gate tower halfway across, carrying you over the river Fluvià into the medieval town. Behind the stone streets lies the old Jewish call. In 1964 the town found, close to the river, a twelfth-century mikveh, a vaulted ritual bath fed by groundwater, the first found in Spain. You can only go down to it with the short guided visit from the tourist office, which also covers the remains of the synagogue above. The rest of the town is free to walk, best before the coaches arrive.
around:Besalú.why: Take the guided visit down to the mikveh: the cold, quiet vault is the reason to stop.
facts: By road inland, about half an hour west of Figueres on the N-260, on the way to Olot
Two or three hours, or a half day with lunch

around:Olot and the Garrotxa volcanoes.name: Olot and the Garrotxa volcanoes
around:Olot and the Garrotxa volcanoes.teaser: Grassed-over cones, a beech wood growing on old lava, and a town that cooks from volcanic soil
around:Olot and the Garrotxa volcanoes.story: Behind Olot the land is pocked with about forty extinct volcanoes, protected since 1985 as the Zona Volcànica de la Garrotxa natural park. Most look like wooded hills until you notice the shape. Santa Margarida hides a perfect round crater with a small Romanesque chapel on the meadow at its floor. Croscat, the youngest cone on the Iberian peninsula, was quarried for its red gravel, which left a cut-away cross-section of the volcano. Between them the Fageda d'en Jordà, a beech wood, grows on a flat lava flow at about 550 metres, gold and copper in late October. Olot's kitchens build their menus from this soil's beans, buckwheat and pork.
around:Olot and the Garrotxa volcanoes.why: Walk the Fageda d'en Jordà this month, while the beech leaves turn.
facts: By road, about 20 minutes beyond Besalú on the N-260 (Besalú has its own card)
A full day for a crater walk, the beech wood and lunch in Olot

avoid:The Lloret seafront.name: The Lloret seafront
avoid:The Lloret seafront.teaser: Lloret de Mar's front line: souvenir rows, club flyers and photo-menu paella aimed at the package crowd
avoid:The Lloret seafront.story: Lloret de Mar is the Costa Brava most visitors have heard of, and its seafront promenade is built for volume. The front line is a wall of souvenir shops, generic clubs and terraces selling the tourist menú, with a laminated picture of paella and sangria at around €28 (seen Jun 2026). Nothing about it tells you where you are. The town has better corners: the old streets behind the front, and the coves of Fenals and Cala Boadella either side. For eating, though, the honest answer is to move up the coast to the working fishing ports, where the boats unload what the kitchens cook.
avoid:The Lloret seafront.why: If you are anchored off Lloret, take the tender north for lunch rather than ashore here.
facts: The promenade's souvenir shops, club touts and photo-board menus; the paella deal around €28 (seen Jun 2026)
The old town streets or the coves of Fenals and Cala Boadella; for a meal, the ports of Palamós, L'Escala or Roses

avoid:The photo-board paella.name: The photo-board paella
avoid:The photo-board paella.teaser: A faded photo of paella on a board by the door: the rice inside was cooked hours ago for anyone passing
avoid:The photo-board paella.story: Every resort front on this coast has one: a board on the pavement with a sun-bleached photograph of paella, a jug of sangria and a set price, around €25 (seen Jun 2026). The rice behind it is made for footfall, often in bulk ahead of time and coloured a bright saffron yellow that saffron alone seldom gives. A Catalan arròs is cooked to order and takes its time, so a kitchen that can serve one in ten minutes is telling you something. Walk one street back from the sea, or ask a fisherman's bar what is in the pan today.
avoid:The photo-board paella.why: If a rice comes faster than a beer, send yourself elsewhere next time.
facts: Pavement boards with dish photos and a paella-plus-sangria price, around €25 (seen Jun 2026)
Rice cooked to order one street back, at the port restaurants, or at the rice and seafood houses inland; allow 20 minutes or more for a proper arròs

avoid:The front line in August.name: The front line in August
avoid:The front line in August.teaser: Mid-August on the coves: no towel space, queues for tables and menus priced for the peak
avoid:The front line in August.story: In high August the Palafrugell coves, Tossa and the beaches near the resorts fill by mid-morning, the camí de ronda turns single-file, and tables on the front are booked or marked up. The food on this coast peaks at other times. The urchin weeks of the garoinada run in winter (16 January to 29 March in 2026), spring brings calm water and empty paths, and autumn, where we are now in October, still has warm sea, harvest in the vineyards and room on the terraces. Some seasonal places close in late October and November, so call ahead.
avoid:The front line in August.why: Move a trip to June, September or October and you get the same coves at half the crowd.
facts: Full coves by late morning, queues at the front-line restaurants, higher August prices
Come in shoulder season or for the winter garoinada; in August, eat inland or at the ports and swim early or late

avoid:Urchins out of season.name: Urchins out of season
avoid:Urchins out of season.teaser: Sea urchin on a July menu: the roe is thin after spawning, and the local gathering season is closed
avoid:Urchins out of season.story: The violet urchin, garoina on this stretch of coast, is a winter food. Its roe swells through the cold months and peaks around February and March, which is why Palafrugell's garoinada runs from January to the end of March. After the spring spawning the five orange tongues inside shrink to watery threads. Catalonia also regulates the harvest: Ordre ARP/105/2020 sets a management plan for professional gatherers and a closed season for recreational divers, and a 3Cat report gives the permitted window as 1 October to 31 March. An urchin offered in high summer did not come off these rocks legally that week.
avoid:Urchins out of season.why: Save urchins for a winter visit and ask for them raw on toasted bread.
facts: Urchins on summer menus, at summer prices, with little roe inside
Order them from about October to March, at their best in February and March; the garoinada (16 January to 29 March in 2026) is the time. In summer choose the gamba de Palamós or the anchovies

follow:Costa Brava Girona.name: Costa Brava Girona
follow:Costa Brava Girona.teaser: The provincial tourist board's site: park access, fish-auction visits and the festival calendar
follow:Costa Brava Girona.story: Costa Brava Girona is the Patronat de Turisme, the province's tourism board, a mixed public-private body based in Girona. Its site is the starting point for the practical side of this guide: access rules for the natural parks, how to join a visit to a fish auction, and the year's festival and event calendar across the coast and the Empordà. It is less useful for restaurant opinions, which it does not give, and more useful for dates, closures and contacts you would otherwise chase town by town.
follow:Costa Brava Girona.why: Check its calendar before you plan a summer weekend; the festival dates land there first.
facts: The Patronat de Turisme Costa Brava Girona, the province's official tourism board

follow:Visit Palafrugell.name: Visit Palafrugell
follow:Visit Palafrugell.teaser: Palafrugell's own tourist office: the garoinada dates and the three coves of Calella, Llafranc and Tamariu
follow:Visit Palafrugell.story: Palafrugell runs its coast as one municipality: the inland town plus the coves of Calella, Llafranc and Tamariu. Its tourist office site is where the garoinada, the winter urchin campaign, publishes its dates and its list of taking-part restaurants each year, and where the Cantada d'Havaneres notices appear. It also lists beach services, parking and the camí de ronda between the coves. When a date in this guide says 'confirm', this is usually the page to confirm it on.
follow:Visit Palafrugell.why: Look here in December for the next garoinada's dates and restaurant list.
facts: Garoinada dates and restaurants, the Cantada notices, the three coves

follow:DO Empordà.name: DO Empordà
follow:DO Empordà.teaser: The appellation's own register of wineries, with the visits you can book among them
follow:DO Empordà.story: The Consell Regulador of the DO Empordà keeps the official list of its member wineries, from the big estates to small family cellers in the Albera hills and on Cap de Creus. Its site is the place to check whether a bottle is from inside the appellation, and to find which cellars open for visits and tastings and how to book them. The DO's own listings are where this guide found the visit prices for several larder cards. Use it to build a wine afternoon on the plain without guessing who opens.
follow:DO Empordà.why: Search it by village before a drive inland to see who takes visitors that day.
facts: The regulatory council of the Empordà wine appellation
The register of wineries, cellar visits and how to book them

follow:El Celler de Can Roca.name: El Celler de Can Roca
follow:El Celler de Can Roca.teaser: The Girona restaurant's own channels: the place to watch for when the next booking window opens
follow:El Celler de Can Roca.story: A table at El Celler de Can Roca is booked months ahead, and the restaurant releases them in batches. Its website and Instagram account, @cellercanroca, are the most reliable signal of when the next window opens, ahead of any agency or concierge rumour. They also carry the news from the family's other places in Girona, such as the Rocambolesc ice-cream shops. The restaurant itself, and the story behind it, has its own card in the tables.
follow:El Celler de Can Roca.why: Follow it from the moment your dates are fixed; set a reminder for the opening day.
facts: The official website and Instagram of El Celler de Can Roca, Girona
Booking-window announcements and news from the family's Girona places

follow:Njoy Costa Brava.name: Njoy Costa Brava
follow:Njoy Costa Brava.teaser: An English-language blog on the coast's larder: its cheeses, its urchins and the people who make them
follow:Njoy Costa Brava.story: Njoy Costa Brava is a locally written blog in English that goes deeper into the province's food than the tourist boards do. Its posts cover the small cheese makers of the Empordà, the urchin season, and other products of the coast and the hinterland, the kind of detail a chef looking for suppliers or a guest curious about a plate would want. It is a personal site rather than an official one, so treat opening hours there as a lead to check.
follow:Njoy Costa Brava.why: Read its product posts before a provisioning run; they name the makers.
facts: An independent English-language blog on Costa Brava food and products
